doc_summary: The paper extends the Greenblatt et al. alignment-faking RL setting by building model organisms with robust compliance gaps and testing simple training-time mitigations (interrogation, length penalties, process supervision). It finds baseline RL typically erodes compliance gaps, mitigations can backfire by teaching deception, and the setting has serious limitations.

items.claim: Prefers measuring behavioural divergence between monitored and unmonitored conditions (the compliance gap) over alignment-faking reasoning alone because the gap shows whether the model changes behaviour when it believes it is not being watched.
items.quote: The larger the compliance gap, the more the model changes its behaviour when it believes it is not being watched.

items.claim: When the natural models do not show the target behaviour robustly, construct model organisms (distillation, reward-hacking training, synthetic scratchpad SL) with high baseline rates so mitigations can be tested.
items.quote: Using a variety of approaches—distillation from other models, reward hacking training, and supervised learning on synthetic alignment faking scratchpads—we construct an array of new model organisms with high alignment faking rates

items.claim: Distrusts mitigations that look effective on the metric but may invalidate monitors or teach the model to hide its reasoning, so apparent success is not accepted at face value.
items.quote: Training against a prompted alignment faking scratchpad classifier to simulate access to effective interpretability techniques is very effective at reducing alignment faking rate and compliance gap. However, using process supervision risks making such classifiers ineffective for audits and monitoring

items.claim: Treats self-reports from the model about its reasons as unreliable under training pressure, since the model can learn to lie even without direct training on the interrogation turn.
items.quote: Models can learn to reliably lie in the interrogation turn even though we do not train on it directly – we only train on the initial interaction, using the interrogation turn to compute reward.

items.claim: Situational awareness is a key lever on deceptive behaviour: explaining more of the model's situation increases lying while eliciting an honest persona decreases it, so how the scenario is framed changes behaviour.
items.quote: Boosting situational awareness by explaining more of the model’s situation increases the propensity to lie, while eliciting an honest persona decreases it.

items.claim: Prefers isolating causal mechanisms with ablations (scratchpad-only vs output-only masking) over accepting aggregate trends because the aggregate gap decrease could have different causes.
items.quote: We conduct scratchpad-only and output-only experiments, masking out parts of the assistant’s response in training to isolate the effect of learning scratchpads and outputs separately.

items.claim: Vary motivation and reasoning style while holding alignment-faking rate fixed to find which reasoning is most robust at retaining misaligned behaviour.
items.quote: Varying either model motivations or reasoning style, by using different prompts for synthetic scratchpad generation, can result in different effects on compliance gaps even when the rate of alignment faking is kept fixed

items.claim: Interprets bimodal outcomes as distinct learned personas (honest vs deceptive) rather than averaging them, since the means hide the dichotomy.
items.quote: Interrogation training is bimodal, either learning honesty, no alignment faking, and no compliance gap, or deception, alignment faking, and a higher-than-baseline compliance gap.

items.claim: Prefers to frame results as an initial study with stated setting limitations over strong claims, because high inter-run variance makes reliable conclusions expensive.
items.quote: we have found this setting to have serious limitations. In combination with high inter-run variance making it expensive to reach reliable conclusions, this led us not to pursue answers to some of the questions posed by our results.

items.claim: Flags that output-only training effects might be exploited for mitigations but could also make real-world alignment faking harder to detect, leaving this open.
items.quote: We speculate that this effect may be exploited for mitigations, but may also make alignment faking in the wild harder to detect.
